newsitem.title: CROATIA: Serbs rally as diplomats visit enclave.
newsitem.headline: Serbs rally as diplomats visit enclave.

text.p: Serbs from the Eastern Slavonia enclave, due to revert to Croatian rule this summer, staged a peaceful rally for a second day on Thursday as Western diplomats visited the region, a U.N. spokesman said.
Philip Arnold told Reuters 800 Serbs had gathered in the enclave's main city of Vukovar on Wednesday and marched peacefully to the local Orthodox church.

"They held similar demonstrations today," Arnold said, but he could not estimate the number, which the Belgrade-based Tanjug news agency put at 8,000. "The basic thrusts (of the protests) is that the area remain a single unit," Arnold added.
The United Nations has endorsed a package Croatia offered to the Serbs and gave Zagreb the green light to go ahead with local election in the enclave, scheduled for March 16.

The Serbs found the package unsatisfactory, demanding that the enclave remain a single administrative unit with more autonomy and not be divided in two counties as envisaged by the Croatian constitution.
Arnold dismissed the demand, put forward by demonstrators in Vukovar. "This has long been overtaken by events," he said.

Eastern Slavonia, which broke away from Croatia in 1991, opposing Zagreb's drive for independence from federal Yugoslavia, is monitored by 5,000 U.N. peacekeepers (UNTAES), whose mandate expires on July 15.
Croatia wants to take full control of the enclave then and return all non-Serb refugees expelled from there since 1991.
A group of diplomats from the United States, Great Britain, France, Russia, Germany, Belgium and Netherlands visited the region on Thursday for talks with UNTAES and Serb officials.
"They emphasized that the (Croat-Serb) agreements are a sound basis for going forward with the election and encouraged the Serbs to stay here and vote," Arnold said.

Tensions were raised in the enclave. A bomb exploded in front of a petrol station retaken by Croatian authorities in the north of the enclave on Wednesday night but no one was injured, the spokesman said.

A Belgian peacekeeper was killed and several others wounded in a shooting attack in the enclave on Saturday. Zagreb blamed the attack on militant Serbs not wishing to accept Croatain rule while the U.N. said it was an isolated criminal act.
Before going to Vukovar U.S. ambassador Peter Galbraith said he would tell the Serbs that "there was no more time for negotiations".
But the international community would ensure that voting was free and fair and that Croatia will meet its obligations afterwards, he said.

The Croatian Foreign Ministry said on Thursday it had issued citizenship papers necessary for voters to 57,000 people or two thirds of the Eastern Slavonia population. The U.N. has put the number of current residents higher, at roughly 120,000.
Many of them are Serb refugees from other rebel enclaves Zagreb retook militarily in 1995.
